title: 1.35, and she feels fine
note: Fictional patient. Your program’s trigger for a creatinine rise, its target levels and the transplant nephrologist’s orders come first.
intro: You are the transplant nurse. Mrs. Rosario Villanueva, 48, received a kidney 14 months ago. Her creatinine has been steady at 1.0 mg/dL. Today it is 1.35. She feels well and wants to get back to work.

choices.text: Yes: a 35% rise from her own baseline. Gather clues before calling.
choices.feedback: Compare with her own baseline, not the laboratory range. With one kidney, a small absolute rise can mean a large loss of function. Gathering the clues first lets the team sort dehydration, drug effect, rejection and other causes in one conversation.

choices.text: Not yet. It is only slightly above the laboratory range and she feels well, so repeat it at her next visit in a month.
choices.feedback: Rejection usually has no symptoms, and the laboratory range is not her baseline. A 35% rise needs evaluation now.
choices.then: You think again and start gathering clues before she leaves.

choices.text: Yes: tell her it may be rejection.
choices.feedback: A creatinine rise triggers an evaluation for rejection and for other causes. It does not establish rejection, and saying so frightens her before anyone knows.
choices.then: She looks frightened. You explain that many things can raise creatinine, and start gathering clues.

n2.scene: No diarrhea, vomiting or new medicines. Her tacrolimus trough, drawn correctly before her dose, is 4.1 ng/mL, lower than her usual. Her urine dipstick shows 2+ protein, new since her last visit.
n2.prompt: How do you ask about her doses?

choices.text: “Many people miss a dose now and then. How many times last month?”
choices.feedback: The normalizing question makes it easier to tell the truth. Shame makes people hide missed doses.
choices.then: She admits the pharmacy ran out of tacrolimus last month. For about five days she took one capsule instead of two to make her supply last.

choices.feedback: A yes-or-no question invites “yes.” Ask in a way that makes missing a dose normal to admit.
choices.then: She says yes. You try the normalizing question, and she admits she stretched her tacrolimus for five days when the pharmacy ran out.

choices.text: Ask her to bring all her medicine bottles next visit so you can count the capsules against the dates.
choices.feedback: A capsule count can help later, but the team needs the answer today. Ask her now, in a way that makes it easy to say.
choices.then: You also ask her now, and she admits she stretched her tacrolimus for five days when the pharmacy ran out.

n3.prompt: What do you tell the transplant nephrologist?

choices.text: Rise from baseline, low trough, the five reduced days, new protein, IgA history, no other clues.
choices.feedback: That is the whole picture in one call: the trend, the level and why it is low, the second signal (protein), the original disease that can recur, and the causes you have already checked.
choices.then: The nephrologist orders donor-specific antibodies, a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, an ultrasound, and a biopsy tomorrow.

choices.feedback: Without her baseline, the level, the missed doses and the protein, the nephrologist has to call back to find out what you already know.
choices.then: The nephrologist asks for the rest. You give it, and she orders tests and a biopsy tomorrow.

choices.text: All the clues, and your suggestion to start pulse steroids today, since missed doses and a low level make rejection likely.
choices.feedback: The clues are right. Treatment is the team’s decision, and the guideline recommends a biopsy before treating rejection unless it would delay treatment substantially.
choices.then: The nephrologist thanks you for the clues and books a biopsy for tomorrow.

n4.scene: At the pre-biopsy check, you ask about every tablet, “including anything from the drugstore or herbal.” She mentions a ginkgo capsule a friend gave her for memory, taken last night.

choices.text: Record the product and last dose, and tell the procedural team before she moves.
choices.feedback: Some herbal products, ginkgo among them, can affect bleeding. Asking by name, with the time of the last dose, finds the risk before the needle. The team decides whether to proceed.
choices.then: The team reviews it with her other results and goes ahead later that morning.

choices.text: Nothing: herbal products are not medicines.
choices.feedback: Herbal products can affect bleeding and drug levels. Report them like any other tablet.
choices.then: You reconsider and tell the procedural team, who review it and go ahead later that morning.

choices.text: Tell her to stop the capsule, and go ahead.
choices.feedback: Stopping it may be sensible later, but whether to proceed today is the procedural team’s decision. Tell them first.
choices.then: You tell the procedural team, who review it and go ahead later that morning.

n5.scene: The biopsy shows T-cell-mediated rejection, and the team starts pulse steroids. After the nephrologist leaves, Mrs. Villanueva cries. “It’s my fault. I killed my kidney.”

choices.text: Rejection found early often responds. Then plan with her for the next pharmacy shortage.
choices.feedback: Explain what rejection is, without predicting the outcome; the nephrologist gives the prognosis. Talk about the missed doses without accusation, and fix the cause: a backup supply, the social worker, and a call to the team before stretching doses.

choices.text: “Don’t worry, the kidney will be fine.”
choices.feedback: You cannot promise that. Say what has been found, what the treatment is for, and when the next results will tell more.

choices.text: “This is why you must never miss a dose. Next time, call us before you change anything, whatever the pharmacy says.”
choices.feedback: The advice is right, but said this way it lands as blame when she is already blaming herself. Shame makes people hide missed doses. Support first, then plan together.

end.title: Six weeks later
end.text: Her creatinine is back to 1.1 mg/dL. The social worker has arranged a backup supplier, and she now has a written plan: if the pharmacy runs out, she calls the transplant team the same day. Her urine protein is followed at every visit, because her original disease can recur.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Compare with her own baseline, not the laboratory range.
  • Gather the clues before you call: volume, drug level and timing, missed doses, infection, obstruction, protein, the original disease.
  • Ask about missed doses in a way that makes the truth easy to say.
  • Ask about every tablet, herbal included, before a biopsy.
  • After the diagnosis, explain without predicting and plan without blame.
